lead: At 1 bar the vapour phase is nearly ideal, so modified Raoult's law works. At 40 bar or 150 bar a gas is dense, its molecules interact, and the vapour fugacity coefficient φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> is far from 1. The liquid standard state and Poynting correction also lose accuracy. High-pressure vapour-liquid equilibrium therefore writes the same fugacity equality, y<sub>i</sub>φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = x<sub>i</sub>φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>, and takes both coefficients from one equation of state. It is how natural gas is processed and separated, how high-pressure absorbers are designed, and how supercritical CO₂ extracts spice oleoresins.
prereq: You need the fugacity criterion from criteria for phase equilibrium and stability, modified Raoult's law from Raoult's law and modified Raoult's law, and cubic equations of state with their mixing rules.

blocks.text: Modified Raoult's law, y<sub>i</sub>P = x<sub>i</sub>γ<sub>i</sub>P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, works near 1 bar because three corrections are hidden and small.

items: The vapour is treated as ideal, so φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = 1.
The liquid standard fugacity is taken as P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>, with Poynting factor exp[V<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>(P − P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>)/(RT)] near 1.

blocks.text: At 40 bar a vapour is dense; φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> can be 0.8 or lower. A component above its critical temperature has no P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>. The Poynting factor grows, and a γ model fitted at low pressure cannot describe a liquid whose density and composition approach the vapour's.

blocks.where: y<sub>i</sub>, x<sub>i</sub> are mole fractions in vapour and liquid; φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup>, φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup> are fugacity coefficients at T, P and phase composition.

blocks.text: The safe route uses one equation of state for both phases. This is the phi-phi method; the gamma-phi method of 6.4 is its low-pressure limit.

sections.h3: K-values from one equation of state

blocks.text: For each component the equilibrium ratio is K<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub>. Divide the fugacity equality by x<sub>i</sub>P:

blocks.where: K<sub>i</sub> is the distribution ratio (dimensionless); values above 1 mean the component prefers vapour.

blocks.text: Use a cubic EOS such as Soave–Redlich–Kwong or Peng–Robinson. Its mixture parameters are a = Σ<sub>i</sub>Σ<sub>j</sub>x<sub>i</sub>x<sub>j</sub>a<sub>ij</sub> and b = Σ<sub>i</sub>x<sub>i</sub>b<sub>i</sub>. The cross term is a<sub>ij</sub> = (1 − k<sub>ij</sub>)√(a<sub>i</sub>a<sub>j</sub>), with k<sub>ij</sub> a fitted binary interaction parameter; for the vapour phase use y<sub>i</sub> in place of x<sub>i</sub>.

Solve the EOS for compressibility factor Z. Take the smallest positive root for liquid and largest for vapour. Put each root and composition into the EOS fugacity expression to get φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup> and φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup>. Both coefficients must come from the same EOS, same k<sub>ij</sub> and same root rule; mixing two models quietly destroys K<sub>i</sub> = φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>/φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup>.

sections.h3: The flash loop, bubble point and dew point

items: Fix T, P and overall composition z<sub>i</sub>.

Estimate K<sub>i</sub> by Wilson: K<sub>i</sub> = (P<sub>c,i</sub>/P) exp[5.373(1+ω<sub>i</sub>)(1 − T<sub>c,i</sub>/T)], with critical pressure P<sub>c,i</sub>, critical temperature T<sub>c,i</sub> and acentric factor ω<sub>i</sub>.

Solve Rachford-Rice Σz<sub>i</sub>(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)/[1 + β(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)] = 0 for vapour fraction β between 0 and 1. Then x<sub>i</sub> = z<sub>i</sub>/[1 + β(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)] and y<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>i</sub>x<sub>i</sub>.
Get φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup> and φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> from the EOS at those compositions. Set K<sub>i,new</sub> = φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>/φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup>.
Return to Rachford-Rice until every K<sub>i</sub> changes by less than the tolerance. Report x<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>, β.

blocks.text: Test the feed before solving Rachford-Rice. With the current K<sub>i</sub>, if Σz<sub>i</sub>K<sub>i</sub> < 1 the feed is a subcooled liquid, and if Σz<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> < 1 it is a superheated vapour; only when both sums exceed 1 does a root β lie between 0 and 1. Near the critical region the EOS loop can also slide to the trivial solution, x<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub> with every K<sub>i</sub> = 1, which satisfies the fugacity equality without being two phases. Reject it and restart from Wilson K-values or a stability test.

Bubble point fixes x and T and solves for P with Σx<sub>i</sub>K<sub>i</sub> = 1. Dew point fixes y and T and solves for P with Σy<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> = 1. Inside the bubble-point loop the trial vapour is y<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>i</sub>x<sub>i</sub>, normalised to sum to 1 before φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> is evaluated; inside the dew-point loop the trial liquid is x<sub>i</sub> = y<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>i</sub>, normalised the same way before φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup> is evaluated.

At high pressure the dew point can be crossed twice. On isothermal compression a gas may condense, then re-vaporise; this is retrograde condensation. Very high pressure can also give gas-gas equilibrium, two dense phases neither of which is a normal liquid. Uses include natural gas and natural gas liquid recovery, high-pressure absorption, and supercritical CO₂ extraction of spices.

figure.caption: The second worked example on the flash loop: Wilson K-values for methane, propane and n-butane at 300 K and 20 bar, the two-phase test, the Rachford-Rice root β = 0.368 (right, where f(β) crosses zero) and the phase compositions. The phi-phi method then updates K from the EOS and repeats.

examples.question: A high-pressure flash at T = 400 K and P = 40 bar is being checked. The trial liquid composition is x₁ = 0.25 and x₂ = 0.75. The equation of state gives φ₁<sup>L</sup> = 0.52, φ₁<sup>V</sup> = 0.88, φ₂<sup>L</sup> = 0.95 and φ₂<sup>V</sup> = 0.97. Find K₁ and K₂. Find S = x₁K₁ + x₂K₂. State what S = 0.8823 means for the bubble point at this temperature.
steps: At a saturated liquid Σy<sub>i</sub> = Σx<sub>i</sub>K<sub>i</sub> = 1. Here S < 1, so this trial liquid is not at its bubble point at 40 bar. At fixed T the bubble-point pressure is below 40 bar; at fixed P the bubble temperature is above 400 K.
examples.answer: K₁ = 0.5909, K₂ = 0.9794 and S = 0.8823; S < 1 means the trial liquid is above its bubble-point pressure at 400 K, and the bubble point lies below 40 bar.
examples.check:
phi1L,phi1V,phi2L,phi2V=0.52,0.88,0.95,0.97
x1=0.25; x2=1-x1
K1=phi1L/phi1V; K2=phi2L/phi2V
S=x1*K1+x2*K2
for v in (K1,K2,S): print(f"{v:.4f}")

examples.question: A gas condensate of methane(1), propane(2) and n-butane(3) with z = 0.30, 0.30, 0.40 enters a flash drum at 300 K and 20 bar. Critical data: methane T<sub>c</sub> = 190.6 K, P<sub>c</sub> = 45.99 bar, ω = 0.012; propane 369.8 K, 42.48 bar, 0.152; n-butane 425.1 K, 37.96 bar, 0.200. Use Wilson K-values to find the vapour fraction β and the phase compositions (the first pass of the loop).
steps: Phase test: Σz<sub>i</sub>K<sub>i</sub> = 0.30 × 16.70 + 0.30 × 0.503 + 0.40 × 0.129 = 5.21 > 1, and Σz<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>i</sub> = 0.018 + 0.596 + 3.100 = 3.71 > 1, so the feed splits into two phases.
Rachford-Rice f(β) = Σz<sub>i</sub>(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)/[1 + β(K<sub>i</sub> − 1)]: f(0) = 4.213, f(0.30) = +0.178, f(0.40) = −0.074. Newton from β = 0.30 gives 0.3609, then 0.3679, then 0.3679 again.
Vapour: y<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>i</sub>x<sub>i</sub> gives y₁ = 0.7393, y₂ = 0.1847, y₃ = 0.0759; the sum is 1.0000.
The full phi-phi method now puts these x and y into the EOS, updates K<sub>i</sub> = φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup>/φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup>, and repeats.
examples.answer: With Wilson K-values (16.70, 0.503, 0.129) the vapour fraction is β = 0.368, the liquid is x = 0.044, 0.367, 0.589 and the vapour is y = 0.739, 0.185, 0.076: methane goes mostly to the vapour, n-butane to the liquid.

traps: Setting φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = 1 at 50 bar. A dense vapour can have φ near 0.7; the error goes straight into K.

Using one EOS for vapour and another for liquid. The equality y<sub>i</sub>φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = x<sub>i</sub>φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup> is then solved with inconsistent φ, so the reported split is not equilibrium.
Choosing the largest Z root for the liquid. The liquid root is the smallest positive root; swapping roots gives K values that may look plausible but are wrong.
Using P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> for a supercritical component. Above T<sub>c</sub> there is no vapour pressure; use the EOS fugacity coefficient instead.

quiz.q: Write the high-pressure VLE fugacity equality and define K<sub>i</sub>.
Why does modified Raoult's law fail at 50 bar even for a simple hydrocarbon mixture?
quiz.a: The vapour is dense, so φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> ≠ 1; the Poynting correction is large; a γ model fitted at low pressure cannot describe the dense liquid near its critical region.

quiz.q: At T and P, φ₁<sup>L</sup> = 0.40, φ₁<sup>V</sup> = 0.80, φ₂<sup>L</sup> = 0.90, φ₂<sup>V</sup> = 1.00 and x₁ = 0.50. Find K₁, K₂ and S = x₁K₁ + x₂K₂.
Why must both fugacity coefficients come from the same EOS and mixing rule?
quiz.a: The equality y<sub>i</sub>φ<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> = x<sub>i</sub>φ<sub>i</sub><sup>L</sup> compares two fugacities on one scale. Different EOS or k<sub>ij</sub> values put the two phases on different scales, so the solved K does not make the fugacities equal.

quiz.q: Explain retrograde condensation using a dew point crossed twice.
quiz.a: On isothermal compression a high-pressure gas reaches a dew point, liquid appears, and further compression can move back into the single-phase region; the dew point is crossed twice. The retrograde liquid is a dense phase, not the ordinary liquid seen at low pressure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gas processing tunes k<sub>ij</sub> in cubic equations, and PC-SAFT handles associating fluids. Search for 'phi-phi flash' and 'retrograde condensation'.
